title: Checkpoint: The Senses
objective: After this level you can explain how the senses gather information and how the brain makes sense of it.
summary: Every sense turns a stimulus into a nerve signal (transduction). Sensation detects; perception interprets. And the brain tunes out what doesn't change: sensory adaptation.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale: you couldn't feel your socks until you read this.
cards.body: Your senses report all day long, yet you don't notice most of it. First, the one trick every sense shares. Then, why your brain stops listening to whatever doesn't change.

cards.headline: Every sense, one trick
cards.body: Every sense starts with specialized receptor cells that turn one kind of stimulus into a nerve signal, a step called transduction. In your retina, photoreceptors do it with light. In your cochlea, hair cells do it with vibration. Taste cells, the smell cells high in your nose and the sensors in your skin do it with chemicals, pressure and heat. Different doors, one currency.

cards.headline: Sensing isn't perceiving
cards.body: Sensation is a receptor detecting something. Perception is your brain organizing and interpreting it into an experience. They aren't the same: Level 69's checkerboard sent your eyes two identical greys, and your brain perceived two different ones. Your receptors collect the data. Your brain writes the story.

cards.fact: You stop noticing what doesn't change.
cards.context: It's called sensory adaptation: we often stop perceiving stimuli that stay the same for a long time. Picture a hotel room with a light flashing steadily outside the window. After a while, you stop noticing it. Your socks are still there too. They've just stopped being news.

mascot.line: Your brain only reads the headlines. Steady things never make the front page.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 complete
learned: More than five senses: how many depends on how you count
Eyes focus light; the brain builds, flips and fills in the picture
Ears sort sound by pitch and keep you balanced
Flavor is taste plus smell; skin senses touch, heat and pain
Receptors sense; the brain perceives, and tunes out what doesn't change

questions.prompt: Senses recap: what is it called when you stop perceiving a stimulus that stays the same for a long time?

options.label: Transduction
options.rationale: That's turning a stimulus into a nerve signal.

options.label: Sensory adaptation
Proprioception
options.rationale: That's your sense of body position.

options.label: Motion sickness
options.rationale: That comes from clashing balance signals.

questions.explanation: Sensory adaptation: we often stop perceiving stimuli that stay relatively constant, like a steadily flashing light.

questions.prompt: Senses recap: what do a photoreceptor in the eye and a hair cell in the cochlea have in common?

options.label: Both focus light onto the retina
options.rationale: Only the cornea and lens focus light.

options.label: Both sense gravity
options.rationale: Grains in the utricle and saccule do that.

options.label: Both grow back every day
options.rationale: Hair cells don't grow back at all.

options.label: Both turn a stimulus into a nerve signal

questions.explanation: Both are receptor cells doing transduction: photoreceptors with light, hair cells with vibration.

questions.prompt: Senses recap: Adelson's two squares send your eyes the same grey but look different. Where does the difference arise?

options.label: In perception: the brain interprets the same input differently
In the cornea, which bends the two squares differently
options.rationale: The cornea bends all the light alike.

options.label: In the cones, which see one square as colored
options.rationale: Both squares are the same grey.

options.label: In the blind spot, which hides one square

questions.explanation: Sensation delivers two identical greys; perception, the brain's interpretation, corrects for the shadow and makes them look different.

questions.prompt: Senses recap, from Level 63: what did DNA from John Dalton's preserved eye reveal in 1995?

options.label: His eye fluid was tinted blue, as he had guessed
He had no rods at all, only cones, in his retinas
options.rationale: His problem was a missing cone pigment gene.

options.label: He lacked the gene for the green-sensitive cone pigment
He had perfectly normal color vision after all
options.rationale: He was color-blind; the DNA showed why.

questions.explanation: DNA from Dalton's preserved eye showed he lacked the gene for the medium-wavelength, green-sensitive cone pigment.

questions.prompt: Senses recap, from Level 66: what is the leading explanation for motion sickness below deck on a ship?

options.label: The inner ear feels motion the eyes can't see
Sea air blocks the smell cells
The ship's noise damages hair cells
options.rationale: Motion sickness comes from clashing signals.

options.label: The eyes see motion the inner ear can't feel
options.rationale: It's the other way round below deck.

questions.explanation: Below deck, the inner ear reports motion while the eyes see a still cabin; that sensory conflict is the leading explanation.
